paragraphs.heading: Frozen seawater that floats
paragraphs.text: Sea ice is what you get when seawater freezes. Ice is less dense than liquid water, so it floats on the ocean, just as ice from fresh water does. Sea ice covers about 7% of Earth's surface and about 12% of its oceans. It is not the same as an iceberg, which is a chunk that breaks off an ice shelf or glacier, although sea ice can have icebergs frozen into it.

paragraphs.heading: Where it lies
paragraphs.text: A large share of the world's sea ice is held in two polar ice packs: the Arctic pack on the Arctic Ocean and the Antarctic pack on the Southern Ocean. Each pack swells and shrinks through the year, spreading widest in winter and pulling back in summer. Whether sea ice is present or not affects shipping routes, local weather and the circulation of the whole ocean.

paragraphs.heading: A cooling lid on the ocean
paragraphs.text: Sea ice matters a great deal for Earth's climate. Its white surface sends sunlight back into space, which helps keep the planet cool; this is called the albedo effect. It also works as a lid, slowing the flow of heat, water vapour and gases such as carbon dioxide between sea and air. Satellites have recorded Arctic sea ice becoming smaller in area and thinner in recent decades, a trend tied to global climate change. Antarctic sea ice varies more from region to region, but it too has started to shrink lately.

paragraphs.heading: Ice, brine and air
paragraphs.text: Sea ice is a mix of pure ice, liquid brine, air and salt. How much of each it holds sets its key properties, such as how well it carries heat, its density and its strength. Inside the ice, salty brine channels are home to microorganisms that form the base of their own food webs. First-year ice usually has a density of about 840 to 910 kg/m³, higher in winter and lower in summer. Getting density wrong is a big source of error when satellites measure ice thickness, adding 0.3 to 0.4 m of uncertainty.

paragraphs.heading: Fast ice and drift ice
paragraphs.text: Wind, currents and changes in water and air temperature keep sea ice on the move and deform it a great deal. One way to sort it is by whether it can drift. Ice frozen to the shore is landfast ice, usually shortened to fast ice. Drift ice lies farther out over very wide areas and moves freely with currents and winds. It is made of floes, separate pieces at least 20 metres across, and floes bigger than 10 km are called giant.

paragraphs.heading: The edge of the pack
paragraphs.text: The drift ice zone splits into a shear zone, a marginal ice zone and a central pack. The marginal ice zone is the band where open ocean gives way to tighter pack ice. There the ice is broken into floes of many sizes. The spread of those sizes shapes how waves and ice interact, how fast ice melts from the sides, and how heat and motion pass between ocean and air.

paragraphs.heading: Ice by age
paragraphs.text: Scientists also sort sea ice by age, through the stages of new ice, nilas, young ice, first-year ice and old ice. New ice is freshly frozen seawater that has not yet become solid. It can take the form of frazil ice, which is plates or needles of ice floating in water, or slush, which is snow soaked with water. It can also be shuga, spongy white lumps a few centimetres wide. Wind and waves gather crystals into forms called grease ice and pancake ice.
